title: Special Permissions
lead: Setuid, setgid and the sticky bit: what they do where plain rwx permissions are not enough (passwd, shared team folders, /tmp). Try them on your own VM, then reinforce in the simulator.
objectives: You recognise the setuid (4), setgid (2) and sticky (1) bits and the leading digit in an octal mode.
You read the letters `s`, `S`, `t`, `T` in `ls -l` output correctly.
You build a team folder with `2775` and explain why new files keep the group.
You protect shared writable folders such as `/tmp` with the sticky bit (`1777`).
You know why setuid is dangerous and audit setuid files with `find`.

sections.title: The three special bits and octal notation
body: Normal permissions are written with three digits (`755`). In the four-digit form the **leading digit** carries the special bits: `4` = setuid, `2` = setgid, `1` = sticky. They add up: `3` = setgid + sticky, `6` = setuid + setgid. A leading zero (`0755`) means no special bit.

`ls -l` shows the bits in the x position: `s` in the owner slot (setuid), `s` in the group slot (setgid), `t` in the others slot (sticky). If the x permission underneath is **missing**, the letter becomes uppercase: `S` or `T`. An uppercase letter means 'bit set, but not executable', which is usually a mistake.

The meaning differs for files and directories: setuid and setgid on a file mean 'run with the owner's/group's privileges'; setgid and sticky on a directory mean 'inherit the group' and 'restrict deletion'.

commands.what: Shows the mode as four-digit octal and as letters.
commands.why: The line `Access: (2775/drwxrwsr-x)` gives both notations side by side.

commands.what: Shows the permissions of the directory itself (not its contents).
commands.where: When checking a team folder or `/tmp`.
commands.why: Without `-d` it lists the contents instead of the directory's own mode.

commands.what: Sets a four-digit octal mode; the leading digit is the special bit.
commands.where: When you want to set a special bit together with the other permissions.
commands.why: You know the exact result, but old special bits are overwritten too.

sections.tip: Symbolic mode is safer: `chmod g+s team` only adds setgid and leaves the other permissions alone.
sections.warn: On files, a three-digit `chmod 755 notes.txt` **clears** the special bits. On directories GNU `chmod` keeps setuid/setgid; to remove them use `chmod g-s team` or the five-digit `chmod 00755`. Check with `ls -ld` afterwards.

sections.title: setuid: run with the owner's privileges
body: When an executable file has **setuid** (`4000`), the program runs with the privileges of the **file owner**, not the person who starts it. The best-known example is `/usr/bin/passwd`: owned by root, shown as `-rwsr-xr-x`. An ordinary user can change their own password because the program, running as root, may update `/etc/shadow`. `sudo` and `mount` work on the same principle.
This power is risky. A small bug in a setuid-root program (or a setuid shell, editor or interpreter) hands root to everyone. That is why you must know your setuid files and audit them regularly.

Two notes: the Linux kernel **ignores** setuid on **shell scripts** (`#!/bin/bash`); `chmod u+s` on a script does not grant root, it only misleads. Also, setuid does nothing on file systems mounted with `nosuid` (e.g. many USB sticks, or a separate `/tmp` partition).

commands.what: Adds setuid in the owner x slot (`s`).
commands.where: Rarely on real systems, only for audited, compiled programs.
commands.why: A (very carefully used) way to let normal users perform one privileged task.

commands.what: Shows the mode of a real setuid program: `-rwsr-xr-x root root`.
commands.where: To see what setuid looks like.
commands.why: The `s` in the owner x slot is setuid.

commands.what: Lists all setuid files on the system (`-perm -4000` = this bit is set).
commands.why: An unexpected setuid file can be a sign of compromise.

sections.tip: Familiar names like `passwd`, `sudo`, `mount`, `su` are normal. An unknown setuid file, or one under `/home` or `/tmp`, needs investigation.
sections.danger: Never run `chmod u+s /bin/bash` (or on vim, python, find, cp) on a real system. It gives every user a root shell and is a classic privilege escalation. At most try it on your isolated test VM, after a snapshot, and undo it afterwards.

sections.title: setgid: a team folder that inherits the group
body: On files, **setgid** (`2000`) runs the program with the group's privileges; in practice its main use is on **directories**. In a directory with setgid, every new file and subdirectory gets the **directory's group** instead of the creator's primary group. New subdirectories inherit the setgid bit too, so the rule holds across the whole tree.

Without it: alice drops a file into the `devs` folder, the file belongs to group `alice`, and teammate bob cannot edit it. With setgid the group stays `devs`. For members to be able to **write** group files you also need `umask 002`; with `022` a new file is `rw-r--r--` and the group cannot write.
The simulator does not implement group inheritance; it only sets the bit and shows it in `ls -l` and `stat`. You will see the real behaviour in the VM task.

commands.what: Adds setgid in the group x slot (`s`).
commands.where: To turn an existing folder into a team folder.
commands.why: Switches on group inheritance without touching other permissions.

commands.what: setgid + `rwxrwxr-x`: owner and group full, others read.
commands.where: When setting up a team folder.
commands.why: The standard team-folder mode in one command.

commands.what: Keeps the group write bit on new files in this shell.
commands.where: Before you work in the team folder.
commands.why: setgid gives the right group, umask lets the group write.

sections.tip: On a directory, `rwxrwsr-x` is fine: group `s` (x present + setgid). With `rwxrwSr-x` the group lacks x and cannot enter the folder; fix it.
sections.warn: `umask` only affects the current shell. To make it permanent add it to the user profile (e.g. `~/.bashrc`); system-wide it is a separate configuration.

sections.title: Sticky bit: restrict deletion in shared folders
body: In a folder everyone can write to (`777`), **anyone can delete or rename other people's files**, because the right to delete depends on the write permission of the directory, not of the file. The **sticky bit** (`1000`) changes that: only the file owner, the directory owner or root may delete or rename.

The classic example is `/tmp`: mode `1777`, shown as `drwxrwxrwt`. Everyone creates files, but nobody deletes someone else's. Sticky matters on **directories**; on files it has no effect on modern Linux.
The simulator does not enforce the deletion protection; you check that the bit is set and appears as `t`. You will try the real protection in the VM with alice and bob.

commands.what: Sets the sticky bit on a directory; `t` appears in the others x slot.
commands.where: On shared, world-writable drop or exchange folders.
commands.why: Stops users from deleting each other's files.

commands.where: When creating a folder everyone may drop files into.
commands.why: The standard shared-folder mode in one command.

sections.tip: An uppercase `T` (`drwxrwx--T`) means sticky is set but others lack x. For a private team folder `1770` can look like this on purpose.

sections.title: Recipe: team folder and what comes next
body: A real team folder is built like this: (1) create the folder, (2) set its group to `devs`, (3) set `2775` (`2770` if outsiders must not read), (4) members work with `umask 002`. Because root creates the folder, you need `sudo`.
If you also want sticky, use `3775` / `3770`: new files belong to the group, and members cannot delete each other's files.

The method has limits: permissions of new files depend on the umask, and you cannot write per-user rules. That is what **default ACLs** (`setfacl -d`) are for, a topic of later modules. For now remember that a setgid folder is the foundation of teamwork without ACLs.

commands.what: Creates the shared folder under `/srv` with root privileges.
commands.where: When setting up a permanent team workspace.
commands.why: A normal user cannot write to `/srv`; sudo is required.
This is the group setgid will pass on.

commands.where: After setting the group, before opening it for use.
commands.why: The group can write and new files get the group `devs`.

sections.warn: Group first, then mode: setting `2775` before the group is `devs` makes the wrong group inherited. At the end `ls -ld` should show `drwxrwsr-x ... devs`.

t01.text: Look at the permissions of `/tmp` with `ls -ld /tmp`. Which letter is at the end?
t01.hint: `drwxrwxrwt`: the final `t` is the sticky bit.

t02.text: Add setuid to `backup.sh` with one command: `chmod u+s backup.sh`.

t03.text: Step by step: set the group of `team` to `devs` with `sudo chgrp devs team`, then apply `chmod 2775 team` and verify with `ls -ld team`.

t04.text: Step by step: look at `drop` with `ls -ld drop`, make it sticky with `chmod 1777 drop`, and run `ls -ld drop` again.

t05.text: Predict: `prog_a` has mode 4755. How do the owner permissions look in `ls -l prog_a`? Guess first, then run it.
t05.hint: x present and setuid set: lowercase `s`.

t06.text: Predict: `prog_b` has mode 4644. How do the owner permissions look? Verify with `ls -l prog_b`.
t06.hint: Owner has no x but setuid is set: uppercase `S`.

t07.text: Predict: `prog_c` has mode 2755. What does the `Access:` line of `stat prog_c` show?
t07.hint: Leading 2 = setgid; in letters the group x slot shows `s`.

t08.text: Debug: someone left setuid (4755) on the shell script `legacy/tool.sh`. The kernel ignores it on scripts, but it fails an audit. Return it to the normal mode `755`.

t09.text: Debug: the folder `inbox` is `777` and users delete each other's files. Fix it to `1777` without touching the existing permissions.

t10.text: Mini project: set the group of `proj` to `devs`, apply `2770` (outsiders locked out), run `umask 002` and create `proj/plan.txt` with `touch`.
t10.hint: Order: `sudo chgrp devs proj`, `chmod 2770 proj`, `umask 002`, `touch proj/plan.txt`.

t11.text: Mini project: create the folder `upload`, set `1777`, put `a.txt` inside and give the file to alice with `sudo chown alice:devs upload/a.txt`. (In reality bob could not delete it.)

t12.text: Challenge: make the folder `release` look like this: group `devs`, setgid set, owner `rwx`, group `r-x`, others nothing.

t13.text: Challenge: which of the three scripts in the folder `audit` have a special bit? Find them and make all of them plain `755`.
t13.hint: Look for `s` with `ls -l audit`. `chmod 755` also clears special bits.

t14.text: TICKET #4501 — The finance team shares the folder `finance`. Files must always belong to group `devs`, the group must be able to write, and outsiders must not get in. Also create the subfolder `finance/2026`.
t14.hint: Group `devs`, mode `2770`: new files get `devs`, others have no access.

t15.text: TICKET #4502 — A developer gave `bin/deploy.sh` setuid so it 'runs as root'. Setuid does not work on scripts and is risky. Remove setuid, set the group `devs` and the mode `750`.
t15.hint: `chmod 750` clears the special bit as well. In practice you grant privileges with a `sudo` rule.

t16.text: TICKET #4503 — A new folder `dropbox` is needed: group `devs`, new files belong to the group, members must not delete each other's files, outsiders cannot enter. Put a `README.txt` inside containing the text `uploads only`.
t16.hint: setgid + sticky = 3, then `770`: `3770`. `echo uploads only > dropbox/README.txt`.

vm.intro: Work on your own Ubuntu/Rocky/Alma VM. The tasks use `/srv` and the temporary users `alice` and `bob`; **take a VM snapshot first**. The first two tasks are read-only, tasks 3–5 create users and folders on the system, and the last one cleans up. Do them in order (3 → 4 → 5).

v01.title: See the special bits
v01.text: Look at the permissions of `/tmp` and of real setuid programs and paste the output.

blocks.expected:
drwxrwxrwt 15 root root 4096 ... /tmp
-rwsr-xr-x 1 root root ... /usr/bin/passwd
-rwsr-xr-x 1 root root ... /usr/bin/sudo
1777 drwxrwxrwt /tmp
4755 -rwsr-xr-x /usr/bin/passwd

differs: If `/usr/bin/sudo` is missing (`No such file`), `sudo` is not installed; no problem, `passwd` is enough.
On some distributions `/tmp` is mounted separately; the mode should still be `1777`.
If you see `ls: cannot access`, find the real path with `which passwd`.

v02.title: Find setuid files on the system
v02.text: List all setuid files and see how many there are.

blocks.cmd:
find / -xdev -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null | head -20
find / -xdev -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null | wc -l

differs: The list depends on the distribution; seeing `passwd`, `mount` or `su` is enough.
If `find` is slow, wait; `-xdev` scans only the main file system, so it is fast.
If you see a path you do not recognise, remember it; in a real audit it would be investigated.

v03.title: Try a setgid folder for real
v03.text: Create the users and group, make one folder with setgid and one without; alice writes into both, then compare the groups.

blocks.cmd:
# TAKE A SNAPSHOT! Temporary users and /srv folders are created
getent group devs || sudo groupadd devs
sudo useradd -m -G devs alice
sudo useradd -m -G devs bob
sudo mkdir -p /srv/project /srv/plain
sudo chgrp devs /srv/project /srv/plain
sudo chmod 2775 /srv/project
sudo chmod 0775 /srv/plain
sudo -u alice touch /srv/project/a.txt /srv/plain/b.txt
ls -ld /srv/project /srv/plain
ls -l /srv/project /srv/plain
blocks.expected:
drwxrwsr-x 2 root devs ... /srv/project
drwxrwxr-x 2 root devs ... /srv/plain
/srv/project:
-rw-r--r-- 1 alice devs ... a.txt
/srv/plain:
-rw-r--r-- 1 alice alice ... b.txt

differs: If you see `useradd: user 'alice' already exists`, the user exists; add it to the group with `sudo usermod -aG devs alice` and continue.
The file in `/srv/plain` should have group `alice`, the one in `/srv/project` group `devs`. If it is the other way round, check the `s` with `ls -ld`.
If `sudo -u alice` fails on Rocky/Alma, check that `sudo` is installed and your user is in `wheel`.

v04.title: Deletion protection with the sticky bit
v04.text: First try, in the sticky folder, to let bob delete alice's file (must fail), then in the folder without sticky (works).

blocks.cmd:
sudo mkdir /srv/pub
sudo chmod 1777 /srv/pub
sudo -u alice touch /srv/pub/alice.txt
sudo -u bob rm -f /srv/pub/alice.txt
ls -l /srv/pub
sudo chmod 777 /srv/pub
sudo -u bob rm -f /srv/pub/alice.txt
ls -l /srv/pub
blocks.expected:
rm: cannot remove '/srv/pub/alice.txt': Operation not permitted
-rw-r--r-- 1 alice alice ... alice.txt
(after removing sticky) total 0

differs: The error message may be translated (`Vorgang nicht zulässig`, `İşleme izin verilmiyor`).
If the file was deleted on the first try, check the `t` with `ls -ld /srv/pub`; was `1777` set?
We use `rm -f` so the 'write-protected' confirmation prompt does not appear.

v05.title: See setuid safely and clean up
v05.text: Give setuid to a copy of the harmless `id` program and see the effect. Then delete all temporary resources.

blocks.cmd:
# ONLY on your own test VM. Never with bash/vim/python!
sudo cp /usr/bin/id /srv/idtest
sudo chmod u+s /srv/idtest
ls -l /srv/idtest
/srv/idtest
blocks.expected:
-rwsr-xr-x 1 root root ... /srv/idtest
uid=1000(youruser) gid=1000(youruser) euid=0(root) groups=...

blocks.cmd:
# Cleanup
sudo rm -f /srv/idtest
sudo rm -rf /srv/project /srv/plain /srv/pub
sudo userdel -r alice
sudo userdel -r bob
ls /srv

differs: If `euid=0(root)` is missing, `/srv` may be mounted `nosuid`; check with `mount | grep nosuid` or try `/usr/local/bin`.
`userdel` may print a mail spool warning; it is harmless.
Delete the group `devs` with `sudo groupdel devs` only if you created it yourself.

q1.q: Which bit makes new files in a team folder get the folder's group?
q1.explain: setgid on a directory passes the directory's group to new files and subdirectories; `2775` is the typical team mode.

q2.q: `/tmp` has mode `1777`. What is the leading `1` for?
options: Only the file owner, directory owner or root may delete
q2.explain: The sticky bit prevents deleting or renaming other people's files in a world-writable folder.

options: setuid is set but the owner has no execute permission
setgid is set and the group can execute
The file has the sticky bit
q3.explain: An uppercase `S` means the bit is set but the underlying x permission is missing; usually a misconfiguration.

q4.q: Which command lists all setuid files on the system?
q4.explain: `-perm -4000` finds files with the setuid bit set; `2>/dev/null` hides permission errors.

summary: In four-digit modes the leading digit is: setuid `4`, setgid `2`, sticky `1`; they add up.
`s`/`t` in the x slot, uppercase `S`/`T` means x is missing.
setuid runs a file with the owner's privileges (`passwd`); the kernel ignores it on scripts; a wrong setuid-root is a serious vulnerability.
setgid folder: new files get the folder's group; team recipe `chgrp devs` + `chmod 2775` + `umask 002`.
Sticky folder (`/tmp`, `1777`): only the owner or root deletes.
Audit setuid files regularly with `find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null`.

glossary.meaning: On executables, the program runs with the owner's privileges; octal `4000`.
On files, run with group privileges; on directories, pass the group to new entries; `2000`.
On directories, only the file/directory owner or root may delete; `1000`.
A normal user gaining root-like privileges without permission.
A mask that decides which permission bits are removed from new files.
Mount option; setuid/setgid are ignored on that file system.
